**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my chest like a stone dropped into a well, rippling outward, darkening the water.

I didn’t know then that some phrases are not just sounds but physical things. That they can press down on your ribs, make it harder to breathe. That years later, you’ll still hear them in the quiet moments before sleep, still feel their ghostly pressure on your sternum.

II.

There’s a myth that writers are born with an overflowing well of words, that we wake up with sentences already formed on our tongues like morning breath. The truth is messier. Most days, I sit in front of a blank screen and think about how much easier it would be to lie down on the floor and stare at the ceiling until the light changes. The cursor blinks like a metronome, counting the seconds I waste.

But then—sometimes—a word arrives. Not a good one, not even the right one, but a word nonetheless. *Hunger.* *Broken.* *Now.* And then another follows, tentative as a deer stepping into a clearing. The sentence is clumsy, half-alive, but it’s *there*. That’s the magic: not the perfection, but the stubborn act of making something from nothing.

III.

I once loved a person who spoke in riddles. They would say things like, *"The sky is a bruise today,"* or *"I dreamt of teeth last night—what does that mean?"* I never knew how to respond. Their words were beautiful, but they left no room for me. I would reach for them and find only mist.

Love, I think, should be a language we both understand. Not poetry, necessarily, but something solid. *"I’m here."* *"I see you."* *"Stay."*

IV.

The internet is a graveyard of words. Tweets deleted in shame, blog posts abandoned mid-sentence, comments typed in anger and never sent. We write more now than ever before, but most of it disappears into the void, unread, unremembered. Sometimes I wonder if that’s why we do it—because the act of writing feels like proof we existed, even if no one bears witness.

I have a folder on my computer labeled *"Things I Can’t Say."* It’s full of letters to people I’ll never send, confessions I’m not brave enough to voice. The files are dated like diary entries: *"March 12 – The Thing About Your Mother,"* *"July 3 – Why I Left,"* *"December 1 – I Miss You (But Not Really)."* Someday, maybe, I’ll set them on fire. Or maybe I’ll forget the password and lose them forever. Both options feel like mercy.

V.

My grandmother had Alzheimer’s. Toward the end, she would look at me with clear, confused eyes and say, *"You’re familiar."* Not *"I know you,"* not *"I love you,"* but *"You’re familiar,"* like I was a song she’d heard once on the radio, long ago. It broke my heart every time.

Words are how we hold onto each other. When they slip away, so do we.

VI.

I read once that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to lie, to hurt, to comfort, to bore, to inspire. 16,000 tiny bricks with which we build or demolish the world around us.

What if we treated them like currency? What if we only spent them on what truly mattered?

VII.

Here’s a secret: I don’t believe in writer’s block. I believe in fear. Fear that the words won’t be good enough, that no one will care, that we’ll say the wrong thing and be exposed as frauds. So we stay silent. But silence is its own kind of lie.

VIII.

When I was a teenager, I wrote terrible poetry in the margins of my notebooks. It was all angst and metaphor—*"my heart is a locked room,"* *"the night is a knife,"* that sort of thing. I cringe now when I read it, but I don’t delete it. Those clumsy, earnest words were the first steps toward figuring out who I was. We all start somewhere.

IX.

The most powerful words are often the simplest. *"Help."* *"Enough."* *"I’m sorry."* They don’t need embellishment. They are complete in their rawness.

X.

I have 1000 words, and I’ve used 800 of them on fragments and half-thoughts. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the weight isn’t in the individual words but in the spaces between them, in what’s left unsaid.

Here’s what I haven’t told you yet:

I’m afraid of being forgotten.
I still think about the dog I had when I was seven.
Sometimes I google my exes to see if they’re happy.
I don’t know how to pray, but I talk to the ceiling anyway.
I want to write something that outlasts me.

XI.

The last word is always the hardest. It has to carry the weight of everything that came before it. It has to feel like an ending, even when it’s not.

So here’s mine:

*Stay.*
